visual_features.color: brown, black, and tan with lighter markings
visual_features.distinctive_marks: distinctive dark rosettes and stripes on the coat

description: The Sunda clouded leopard (Neofelis diardi) is a medium-sized wild cat native to Borneo and Sumatra. It was only identified as a separate species from the mainland clouded leopard (Neofelis nebulosa) in 2006 based on genetic research showing differences in mtDNA, nuclear DNA sequences, and microsatellite and cytogenetic variation. The two species diverged between 2 and 0.9 million years ago. Two subspecies are recognized: the Bornean clouded leopard (N. d. borneensis) and the Sumatran clouded leopard (N. d. diardi), which diverged during the Middle to Late Pleistocene around the time of the Toba super-eruption 69,000-77,000 years ago. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List and on CITES Appendix I, with the total effective population probably fewer than 10,000 mature individuals.
population_estimate: Total effective population estimated at fewer than 10,000 mature individuals with a decreasing trend. In Sabah, the population is roughly estimated at 1,500-3,200 individuals, with only 275-585 living in protected reserves large enough for long-term viability. Density on Borneo ranges from 0.8 to 4.4 individuals per 100 km² across different forest types. On Sumatra, density is much lower at about 1.29 individuals per 100 km², possibly due to competition with Sumatran tigers. Density outside protected areas on Borneo is estimated at approximately 1 individual per 100 km².
habitat: Restricted to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra. In Borneo, it inhabits lowland rainforest and logged forest below 1,500 m elevation. In Sumatra, it appears more abundant in hilly, montane areas. Records exist from Kerinci Seblat, Gunung Leuser, and Bukit Barisan Selatan National Parks. The species is strongly arboreal and entirely forest-dependent. Clouded leopard fossils have also been found on Java, where it likely became extinct during the Holocene.
threats: Deforestation - Borneo has one of the world's highest deforestation rates, with forest cover declining from nearly 75% in the mid-1980s to 52% by 2005
Habitat fragmentation due to forest conversion for oil palm and timber plantations
Poaching for pelts, canines, claws and live trade - between 2011-2019, body parts of 32 individuals were seized in Indonesia
Forest fires, particularly in Kalimantan and Sebangau National Park
Small protected populations - only 275-585 individuals in reserves large enough for long-term viability on Borneo
ecosystem_role: As Borneo's largest terrestrial predator (and a top predator on Sumatra alongside the tiger), the Sunda clouded leopard plays a crucial role in regulating prey populations including sambar deer, muntjacs, Bornean bearded pigs, mouse deer, porcupines, and primates. By controlling herbivore numbers, it helps maintain forest health and regeneration. Its secretive, largely solitary nature makes it difficult to study, but its presence is a key indicator of intact, healthy forest ecosystems with sufficient prey populations.
human_connection: The Sunda clouded leopard holds cultural significance in parts of its range - its Indonesian name 'rimau-dahan' means 'tree tiger' or 'branch tiger'. It was only recognized as a unique species in 2006, highlighting how much we still have to learn about Borneo and Sumatra's biodiversity. It serves as a flagship species for forest conservation in Borneo through the Bornean Wild Cat and Clouded Leopard Project. Illegal trade threatens the species - in 2019 a live individual seized in Jakarta had been ordered by a Kuwaiti buyer. The species' survival depends on protecting remaining forest corridors between protected areas.
what_students_can_do: Learn about the link between deforestation in Southeast Asia and the loss of predator species like the Sunda clouded leopard
Support certified sustainable palm oil (RSPO) and wood products
Raise awareness about illegal wildlife trade and avoid purchasing products made from wild cat parts
Support research and conservation organizations working to protect Bornean and Sumatran forests
Reduce paper consumption to help decrease pressure on forest habitats
fun_fact: The Sunda clouded leopard wasn't recognized as a separate species from the mainland clouded leopard until 2006 - DNA analysis revealed they had been evolving separately for up to 2 million years!

Despite being called a 'leopard', the Sunda clouded leopard is not closely related to true leopards - its closest relatives are all in the genus Neofelis, and it split from the big cat lineage about 6 million years ago.
This cat has the longest canine teeth relative to its skull size of any living cat - its 5.1 cm fangs are proportionally similar to those of the extinct saber-toothed tiger.
